$comment: CCAO-F question bank, authored at S4 (exam-author) per methodology/03-authoring-guide.md from content/ccao-f/{concepts.json,authoring.json,manifest.json,syllabus-rules.json,derivation/} ONLY (clean-room). Every concept is the primary concept of exactly one item; themes are the CCAO-F T1-T8 set in authoring.json; distractor tags reference methodology/distractor-patterns.json + extensions E01/E02. Style: vendor card in derivation/source-ccas-guide-samples.md (en-US, scenario stems, generic roles, stated deciding constraint, superlative framing, option-length parity).

questions.question: A banquet sales coordinator at a hotel banquet and catering sales office is setting up a prompt that will draft proposals for wedding clients. A colleague shares a long template prompt admired across the team for its confident, polished wording, and the coordinator must decide what standard to judge a prompt against before adopting one. Which standard is the most appropriate?

options.A: Judge a prompt by whether the proposals it produces are fit for the business purpose the team needs
options.B: Adopt the shared template on the strength of the results colleagues across the team vouch for
options.C: Judge the prompt by how confident and polished the drafts it returns sound on a first read
options.D: Prefer the longest, most detailed prompt available, since detailed prompts are accepted best practice

rationale.correct: A prompt is a specification: it states the work, the inputs that govern it, and what a good result looks like, and its quality is judged by the output's fitness for the business purpose — effective prompts are measured against the proposal the team actually needs, not against length or register.

distractors.B: A colleague's endorsement is an anecdote, not a measure; the template still has to be judged against the output it produces for this team's proposals.
distractors.C: Confident, polished wording is a register, not a fitness signal; a fluent draft can still miss what the client asked for.
distractors.D: Length is not a quality standard; a long prompt that never states what a good result looks like is a weaker specification than a short one that does.

questions.question: A program associate at an airline loyalty program office asks Claude to draft a member communication about changes to tier benefits. The prompt assigns a role, pastes the briefing document as context, and states the task. The draft comes back well written, but it runs far past the required two-page limit and arrives as flowing prose instead of the required benefits table. Which TWO changes to the prompt would most directly address the problem? (Select TWO.)

options.A: State the constraints the draft must respect, including the two-page limit
options.B: Assign a more senior-sounding role so the draft takes on an executive register
options.C: Specify the format the output must arrive in, naming the required benefits table
options.D: Convert the prose into the benefits table by hand after each draft arrives
options.E: Ask Claude to review its own draft and correct any problems it can find

rationale.correct: The five components — role, context, task, constraints, format — run as a checklist. This prompt already carries a role, context, and the task, and the two failures map exactly onto the two missing components: constraints, which own the two-page limit, and format, which owns the benefits table. Naming both fixes the specification, where the correction holds for every future draft.

distractors.B: A role changes register, not correctness; it is one component of five and cannot substitute for the missing constraints and format.
distractors.D: Reformatting by hand treats the symptom each time while the prompt keeps producing prose; the missing components stay missing.
distractors.E: Self-review runs inside the context that produced the draft; it cannot supply constraints and format the request never stated.

questions.question: A content officer at a regional tourism board asks Claude to draft social posts promoting the spring campaign. The drafts come back grammatical and on topic, yet generic enough to fit any destination. The officer knows the campaign's audience, hook, and headline events well, none of which appear in the request, and is close to concluding the model cannot handle marketing work. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Move the task to the most capable model tier and run the same request again
options.B: Add the audience, hook, and headline events the request never stated, then rerun it
options.C: Keep the drafts and hand edit distinctive local detail into each post after every run
options.D: Take campaign writing back from the tool and produce the posts manually from now on

rationale.correct: Claude cannot see what exists only in the requester's head, so generic, on-topic output is diagnosed as a context gap before it is blamed on a model limitation. Supplying the audience, hook, and headline events closes the gap the drafts are exposing.

distractors.A: Upgrading capability does not supply the missing campaign specifics; a stronger tier fills the same gap with better-worded generic material.
distractors.C: Hand editing rewrites the symptom on every run while the request keeps omitting what makes the campaign distinct.
distractors.D: Walking away treats a fixable context gap as a permanent limitation; nothing here shows the task is beyond the tool.

questions.question: A grants officer at a charity grant administration team delegates a monthly job to Claude: screen applications against eligibility criteria, check each budget against policy limits, and draft a funding memo. Run as one large prompt, the memos read smoothly — but when one is wrong, the officer cannot tell which part of the job failed. What is the most appropriate way to restructure the work?

options.A: Split the job into ordered steps and check each stage's result before the next stage consumes it
options.B: Keep the single prompt and expand it with more detailed instructions covering every stage
options.C: Commission an automated multi-agent pipeline in which each stage is handled by its own agent
options.D: Keep the current prompt and pass the memos that read fluent and complete without further checks

rationale.correct: Task decomposition techniques split complex work into ordered steps, each producing a checkable result before the next step consumes it. Checkable intermediates are what make delegated multi-stage work diagnosable: when a memo is wrong, the failing stage is visible instead of buried in one opaque pass.

distractors.B: More instructions make the single prompt longer, not more diagnosable; a failure still cannot be traced to a stage.
distractors.C: An agent pipeline adds machinery a monthly three-stage job does not warrant, and building one sits beyond an Associate's scope besides.
distractors.D: Fluent, complete-sounding memos are not evidence of correctness; the officer already knows some of them are wrong.

questions.question: A project lead at a market research fieldwork agency has decomposed a client study into steps: design the questionnaire, build the fieldwork schedule, brief the interviewers, and draft the client summary. Every later step depends on the questionnaire, and the client is eager to see something polished early. Which step should the lead build with Claude and verify first?

options.A: The client summary, because a polished early deliverable is what the client is waiting to see
options.B: The interviewer briefing, leaving the questionnaire for the end when requirements are clearest
options.C: The questionnaire, verified before any later step is allowed to build on top of it
options.D: All four steps in a single pass, keeping the study whole instead of fragmenting it into stages

rationale.correct: How to structure complex requests is decided by dependency and stakes: the step everything else rests on is built and verified first, because every later step inherits its errors. The questionnaire governs the fieldwork schedule, the interviewer briefing, and the client summary alike.

distractors.A: A polished early deliverable is client optics, not a build order; a summary drafted before the questionnaire exists rests on nothing.
distractors.B: Deferring the load-bearing step compounds its cost; a briefing built without the questionnaire will need redoing once it exists.
distractors.D: Running the study as one undivided pass removes the checkpoints the decomposition just created and makes failures untraceable again.

questions.question: An operations coordinator at a dental clinic network runs one long-standing prompt that produces patient recall letters, drafts follow-up scheduling blocks, and assigns insurance codes in a single pass. Output is intermittently wrong, and the coordinator cannot tell which of the three functions produces the errors. What is the most appropriate change?

options.A: Keep the prompt and correct whichever letters, blocks, or codes turn out wrong after each run
options.B: Tighten the prompt's wording and reduce the latitude it grants, leaving its structure as it is
options.C: Retire and rewrite the prompt periodically, as prompts accumulate errors the longer they are reused
options.D: Restructure the single prompt into separate stages so each function returns its own result

rationale.correct: A single opaque prompt covering many stages cannot be diagnosed when it fails. The remedy for complex requests is decomposition: each function returns a result that can be checked on its own, so errors become attributable to a stage instead of hiding somewhere in one pass.

distractors.A: Correcting outputs downstream treats the symptoms one at a time while the source of the errors stays unlocated.
distractors.B: Wording and latitude are knobs; neither makes a three-function prompt traceable, and the failing function stays hidden.
distractors.C: Prompts do not accumulate errors with reuse; that claim invents a mechanism, and a rewritten monolith is exactly as undiagnosable.

questions.question: An agent at a corporate travel desk uses Claude to summarize the company travel policy for new hires. The first draft is accurate but comes back at twice the length requested. On earlier tasks the agent responded to a flawed draft by rewriting the entire prompt from scratch, and the results swung unpredictably between rounds. What is the most appropriate way to run the next round?

options.A: Read the draft as a diagnostic, identify the one component it points at, and change only that
options.B: Rewrite the role, context, and format lines together so the next round improves on every front at once
options.C: Swap in a prompt another team praises for its policy summaries and run that one instead
options.D: Stop iterating and write the summary by hand, treating the over-long draft as the tool's ceiling

rationale.correct: The output is read as a diagnostic naming which component of the request failed — an accurate draft at twice the length requested points at the length constraint — and exactly one component changes per round, so the effect is attributable. That is how to iterate prompts toward better quality without the swings whole-prompt rewrites produce.

distractors.B: Changing several components at once means no improvement or regression can be attributed to any of them — the same confounding the from-scratch rewrites produced.
distractors.C: Another team's admired prompt is an anecdote about a different task; adopting it discards the diagnostic the current draft just supplied.
distractors.D: One over-long draft is not a capability ceiling; the output points at a fixable component, not at the tool.

questions.question: A marketing coordinator at an independent bookstore chain has spent five rounds rewording a prompt for a staff-picks newsletter that must cite each store's monthly sales figures. Improvement stopped at round three: the drafts remain fluent, the figures are still invented, and no sales data has ever been attached to the request. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Run a further round of still more elaborate wording spelling out exactly what the drafts should contain
options.B: Stop rewording and attach the monthly sales figures the newsletter must cite
options.C: Move the task to the most capable model tier and rerun the current prompt unchanged
options.D: Conclude the newsletter cannot be delegated and return to writing it manually each month

rationale.correct: Iteration terminates: when successive rounds stop improving the result, the remaining gap is a task or evidence problem, not a wording problem. The drafts invent figures because no sales data was ever supplied, and attaching the monthly sales figures closes a gap no phrasing change can reach.

distractors.A: Improvement already stopped at round three; more elaborate wording keeps working on a component that is not the problem.
distractors.C: A more capable tier cannot cite data it was never given; the invented figures are an evidence gap, not a capability gap.
distractors.D: Delegation is not the failure; a request without the sales data could never have succeeded, and supplying it has not been tried.

questions.question: A triage administrator at a veterinary clinic group uses Claude to sort incoming owner messages into urgent and routine queues. The category definitions in the prompt are already thorough, and clear-cut messages sort correctly — but borderline messages, like an older dog refusing one meal or a cat hiding since yesterday, keep landing in the wrong queue. What is the most appropriate revision?

options.A: Extend the definitions with additional paragraphs describing each category in finer detail
options.B: Ask owners to mark their own messages as urgent or routine when they write in
options.C: Add worked examples of borderline messages, each labeled with the correct queue
options.D: Have staff re-sort the borderline messages by hand at the end of each day

rationale.correct: When definitions are already adequate and boundary cases still fail, the missing component is worked examples that mark the boundary. Labeled borderline cases show where the line sits, which more definition cannot — the reliable way to improve output quality on edge cases.

distractors.A: The definitions are not the failing component — clear-cut messages already sort correctly; more definition is the wrong fix for boundary cases.
distractors.B: Pushing the classification onto owners makes the failure the user's problem and hands the triage call to the least qualified party.
distractors.D: A daily hand re-sort treats the symptom after the queue damage is done and leaves the prompt misrouting tomorrow's messages.

questions.question: A development associate at an orchestra development office uses one heavily constrained prompt template — fixed structure, fixed tone, fixed length — for every task. It performs well on donor-report analysis, but when the associate uses it to brainstorm next season's fundraising campaign themes, every run returns the same three predictable ideas. What is the most appropriate adjustment?

options.A: Keep maximum constraints on every task, as tightly specified prompts are accepted best practice
options.B: Reuse whichever prompt produced last year's most admired campaign and adapt its wording
options.C: Drop the constraints from every task's prompt so that no request is over-specified again
options.D: Keep the constraints for the analysis work and grant the brainstorming prompt deliberate latitude

rationale.correct: Task type sets how much latitude the prompt grants: convergent analysis is constrained, divergent brainstorming is deliberately left open. Control and range trade off, and one prompt cannot maximize both — the fixed template is right for donor-report analysis and wrong for campaign brainstorming.

distractors.A: Tight specification is not a universal best practice; applied to divergent work, it is exactly what keeps returning the same three predictable ideas.
distractors.B: Last year's admired campaign is an anecdote; copying its prompt neither diagnoses the template nor sets latitude by task type.
distractors.C: Removing constraints everywhere trades one mismatch for another: the donor-report analysis needs the control the template currently provides.

questions.question: An export desk coordinator at a furniture manufacturer asks Claude for a polished briefing on current import duties in two target markets, prompting it exactly as they would for drafting work: a role, the audience, and a request for finished prose. The briefing comes back reading authoritative. What is the most appropriate way to handle this task?

options.A: Accept the briefing as finished; its authoritative, polished register shows the duties are reliable
options.B: Treat the job as a research task first, grounding the duties in current sources before any drafting
options.C: Rely on the model's training staying current, as duty rates are refreshed into it when they change
options.D: Publish now and schedule a quarterly hand check to catch any duty figures that have gone stale

rationale.correct: The four task types — analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming — each fail in a characteristic way when the wrong strategy is applied. Import duties in two target markets are a research task type: current information must be brought to the task first, and drafting begins only once the facts are grounded.

distractors.A: An authoritative register is fluency, not currency; polished prose is exactly how a drafting strategy dresses stale or invented duty figures.
distractors.C: Pretrained knowledge carries no currency guarantee, and no mechanism refreshes duty rates into it as they change; that claim invents one.
distractors.D: A quarterly check detects damage after the briefing has circulated; a research task needs facts grounded before drafting, not audited after.

questions.question: A program coordinator at an apprenticeship training provider uses Claude to draft employer progress reports, some routine and some feeding funding decisions. The coordinator is writing the team's standing evaluation step for these drafts and wants it to hold for both kinds of report. Which evaluation discipline is the most appropriate?

options.A: Check each draft against the requirements, the source material, and professional standards, varying only depth of review
options.B: Pass the routine drafts on how complete and well organized they read, saving real checks for the funding reports
options.C: Pick which of the three references to check on each draft according to the time available that week
options.D: Send all drafts out and review a weekly sample of them against the source material after the fact

rationale.correct: Evaluation runs against three explicit references every time — the requirements, the source material, and professional standards. What flexes with the stakes is the depth of review, never the reference set, which is exactly what lets one standing step cover routine and funding reports alike.

distractors.B: How complete a draft reads is register, not evaluation; skipping the references on routine work is where unchecked errors settle.
distractors.C: Time pressure calibrates depth, not the reference set; dropping a reference removes a check the discipline says always runs.
distractors.D: A weekly sample reviews damage after reports have gone out; evaluation belongs before release, at a depth matched to the stakes.

questions.question: An analyst at an employee benefits consultancy has Claude draft a renewal comparison memo for a client choosing between two health plans. The analyst fact-checks every figure and every plan feature named in the memo and finds them all accurate. The client will decide directly from this memo. What should the analyst do before sending it?

options.A: Send it: every claim in the memo has been verified, so the evaluation is finished
options.B: Check the memo against the full set of items the renewal decision needs, looking for what is absent
options.C: Ask Claude to list anything it may have left out of its own memo and send once it reports nothing
options.D: Send it now and rely on the client's follow-up questions to surface anything that is missing

rationale.correct: Completeness is a separate check from accuracy: a memo can be entirely true and still omit what the decision needs, and the omission is silent — nothing present flags what is absent. The memo is checked against what the renewal decision requires, not only against whether its claims hold.

distractors.A: Verifying the claims that are present assumes completeness without checking it; accuracy checks cannot flag an absent item.
distractors.C: The same context that produced the omission cannot be relied on to see it; a clean self-report is not a completeness check.
distractors.D: Waiting for client questions pushes the gap onto the person the memo was supposed to equip, after the decision is already in motion.

questions.question: A supervisor at an insurance claims intake team is rolling out Claude to draft claim acknowledgment and status letters that go out under the supervisor's name. A teammate asks who is answerable if a drafted letter misstates a policyholder's coverage position. Which working assumption is the most appropriate?

options.A: Add a notice to each letter that it was drafted with AI assistance so responsibility is shared with the tool
options.B: Withdraw Claude from policyholder correspondence so the question of ownership never arises
options.C: Treat every claim in each letter as the supervisor's own and review it accordingly before it ships
options.D: Route every drafted letter to the legal department for sign-off so accountability moves upstream

rationale.correct: Accountability is non-delegable: the sender owns every claim in what they ship regardless of who or what drafted it. That ownership is why review is sized to the letter, and it is the reason output evaluation carries the largest weight in this credential.

distractors.A: A disclosure notice informs the reader; it does not move ownership of a misstated coverage position off the sender.
distractors.B: Removing the tool answers a governance question by giving up the capability; ownership of shipped claims was never in doubt.
distractors.D: Routing routine letters to legal hands the supervisor's own call away; the deciding evidence sits with the sender, not upstream.

questions.question: An associate at a private wealth client reporting desk has Claude draft a quarterly letter that cites a specific benchmark return and the effective date of a new reporting regulation. The letter goes to clients who act on it. The draft reads clean and the model, asked directly, rates its own confidence as high. What must happen before the letter is sent?

options.A: Send it: the model's high confidence rating covers the two specifics it cited
options.B: Have Claude re-examine its own draft and confirm the return and the date before sending
options.C: Soften the two specifics into approximate language so no precise claim is on record
options.D: Validate the benchmark return and the effective date against the authoritative sources

rationale.correct: Fabricated specifics — numbers, names, dates presented in the register of fact — are the hallucinations that matter most here, and a checkable specific bound for a consequential audience is validated against the authoritative source before it leaves your hands.

distractors.A: A self-reported confidence rating is not an accuracy signal; fabricated specifics arrive in exactly this confident register.
distractors.B: Re-examination by the context that produced the draft anchors to the same assumptions; it is not validation against a source.
distractors.C: Hedging the language treats the symptom: clients still act on the letter, and the underlying claims remain unverified.

questions.question: A researcher at an executive search firm has Claude compile a background brief on a shortlisted candidate. Asked directly how confident it is, the model answers that it is highly confident, and the brief reads polished and specific. The brief goes to the client panel tomorrow. Which verification approach is the most appropriate?

options.A: Accept the brief on the strength of the model's stated confidence and its specific, polished detail
options.B: Check the brief's load-bearing claims against authoritative records before it goes to the panel
options.C: Ask the model to re-read the brief and flag anything it is unsure about, then send it as cleared
options.D: Rely on the model flagging uncertain claims automatically, so an unflagged brief stands verified

rationale.correct: Fluency, confidence, and the model's self-assessment are not accuracy signals — confident uncertainty is a named risk, and fact-checking and validation techniques mean checking claims against an authoritative source, never against the output's register or a confidence report.

distractors.A: Stated confidence and polish are register; a brief can carry both while misstating the claims the panel will act on.
distractors.C: A self-read by the producing context is not verification; unsure claims are exactly what it fails to see as unsure.
distractors.D: No mechanism guarantees uncertain claims arrive flagged; treating unflagged as verified invents a safeguard that does not exist.

questions.question: A communications officer at a public health outreach unit uses Claude to draft campaign materials for different neighborhoods. The team's review step checks accuracy and formatting. Over several weeks, the drafts keep framing the same neighborhoods around risk and the same others around wellness, and each draft has passed review. What is the most appropriate change to the process?

options.A: Add bias and fairness checks to the routine review that every draft already goes through
options.B: Rely on the platform's built-in safeguards, which prevent biased material from being generated
options.C: Commission a quarterly audit of published materials to look for patterns across neighborhoods
options.D: Wait for community feedback to identify any framing problems before changing the review

rationale.correct: Bias detection belongs in the routine review of ordinary outputs, not in a separate exercise reserved for sensitive work. An output can be accurate and well formatted and still unfair — these drafts passed both checks — and routine review is what catches the framing pattern before it publishes.

distractors.B: No built-in safeguard guarantees fair framing of neighborhoods; the claim invents a protection the drafts are already defeating.
distractors.C: A quarterly audit finds the pattern after months of publication; the review step touches every draft before it ships.
distractors.D: Community feedback is the lagging signal — it arrives from the people the framing harmed, weeks after review could have caught it.

questions.question: A broker at an import customs brokerage asks Claude which duty classifications apply to a client's new product line. Several relevant classifications were revised two months ago, and the broker knows rulings in this area change frequently. What is the most appropriate way to get a usable answer?

options.A: Add an instruction telling the model to make certain every classification it lists is current and accurate
options.B: Use the model's answer as given, as it is written in the same assured register as the official schedule
options.C: Postpone the classification work until a model version with more recent training becomes available
options.D: Supply the current rulings or retrieve them from an authoritative current source, then validate the answer against them

rationale.correct: Pretrained knowledge carries no currency guarantee: facts that change quickly, like classifications revised two months ago, are supplied or retrieved from an authoritative current source and then validated. Validation against that source is what makes the answer usable — asking the model to try harder does not create currency.

distractors.A: An exhortation to be current changes nothing the model can draw on; no instruction creates knowledge it does not hold.
distractors.B: An assured register is not currency; stale classifications arrive written exactly like fresh ones.
distractors.C: Waiting defers the client's work and still ends at a training cutoff; the ruling source is available now.

questions.question: A compliance specialist at a pharmacy chain compliance team uses Claude with an uploaded pack of current state regulations to draft store-level compliance summaries. Fabricated regulatory detail in a summary would be costly, and the specialist wants the protection built in at request time. Which TWO prompt provisions most directly reduce that risk? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Instruct the model to be thorough, professional, and as accurate as possible in every summary
options.B: Permit an explicit "I don't know" whenever the uploaded pack does not answer the question
options.C: Schedule a careful post-draft fact-check of each summary against the pack before filing
options.D: Restrict all claims to the uploaded pack and require auditable citations to it for each claim
options.E: Ask the model to attach a confidence score to every claim so weak ones stand out

rationale.correct: Verification is cheapest when built into the request: permit an explicit "I don't know" so gaps surface as gaps, restrict to sources so claims cannot wander beyond the pack, and require auditable citations so every claim can be traced. Prevention at request time beats reconstruction at review time.

distractors.A: Thoroughness and accuracy exhortations adjust register, not mechanism; they build no verification into the request.
distractors.C: A post-draft fact-check is reconstruction at review time — legitimate, but it is the expensive backstop, not the request-time protection asked for.
distractors.E: Self-assigned confidence scores are the model grading its own claims; a fabricated specific can carry a high score.

questions.question: A customer success manager at a b2b software company prepares quarterly business reviews from a raw usage export. Claude drafts the narrative well, and the manager has also been letting it state the renewal metrics — totals and percentage changes — directly in the prose. The client's renewal hinges on those figures. What is the most appropriate way to produce the metrics?

options.A: Generate the metrics twice in separate runs and keep the figures both runs agree on
options.B: Paste the usage export into the prompt twice so the model has more chances to read it correctly
options.C: Have the metrics computed from the export with code execution and generate only the narrative around them
options.D: Keep generating the metrics in prose and hand-verify each figure in the finished deck every quarter

rationale.correct: Where numbers must be right they are computed rather than generated as prose: generation supplies language, computation supplies figures, and which of the two produced a number decides how far it can be trusted. Code execution turns the renewal metrics into computed results instead of plausible prose.

distractors.A: Agreement between two generated runs measures consistency, not correctness; both runs can misstate the same total.
distractors.B: Duplicating the export adds volume, not arithmetic; the figures are still generated as prose either way.
distractors.D: Quarterly hand-verification is a detective backstop for a number that could simply have been computed correctly at the start.

questions.question: A sales support lead at a medical device sales support team is writing the standing rule for when Claude-drafted materials must receive human review before going out, so the decision is settled in advance rather than argued at each deadline. Which TWO factors belong in that rule? (Select TWO.)

options.A: How fluent and confident the finished draft reads when the team skims it
options.B: Which model tier produced the draft, since more capable tiers need less review
options.C: The stakes of the material and how reversible the communication is once sent
options.D: The time remaining before the material's send deadline on the day
options.E: The audience receiving the material and the regulatory exposure it carries

rationale.correct: The human-review threshold is decided in advance from four factors — stakes, reversibility, audience, and regulatory exposure. Writing those factors into the standing rule is what keeps the review decision from being renegotiated at the moment of sending under time pressure.

distractors.A: A draft's fluent register says nothing about what its errors would cost; confident drafts are the ones that slip through.
distractors.B: No tier confers immunity from review; the claim turns a capability difference into a safeguard it does not provide.
distractors.D: Deadline pressure is precisely what the advance rule exists to overrule; time remaining is not a review criterion.

questions.question: A donor relations manager at a nonprofit uses Claude to draft gift acknowledgment letters containing tax receipt language, a category the organization classes as requiring mandatory review. Currently an intern skims each letter for tone, without access to the donation records. What is the most appropriate way to discharge the review obligation?

options.A: Route the letters to a reviewer qualified on receipt requirements, with the donation records at hand
options.B: Keep the intern's sign-off, as having a human in the loop is what mandatory review requires
options.C: Replace the review step with a printed line disclosing that the letter was drafted with AI assistance
options.D: Have Claude verify the receipt language and amounts itself before the intern signs each letter

rationale.correct: Mandatory review means a qualified reviewer with access to the evidence. A tone skim without the donation records is a rubber stamp: human review that cannot see the amounts or judge the receipt language does not discharge the obligation, however sincere the reviewer.

distractors.B: A human in the loop is a slogan, not the standard; an unqualified, evidence-blind sign-off leaves the obligation undischarged.
distractors.C: Disclosure tells the donor how the letter was made; it fixes nothing about whether the receipt language is right.
distractors.D: The tool checking its own draft is review inside the producing context; the obligation calls for independent, qualified eyes.

questions.question: An outreach coordinator at a city library team has a fully verified annual-report summary and asks Claude to adapt it for a council briefing — plainer vocabulary, less detail, sharper framing for the intended audience. In the adapted version, a carefully qualified usage statistic now reads as a stronger, simpler claim. What is the most appropriate handling?

options.A: Send the adaptation as is: the source summary was verified, and verification carries through adaptation
options.B: Re-run the full evaluation from scratch on every audience variant the team ever produces
options.C: Keep claims intact when adapting, and re-verify the usage statistic whose claim changed in the rewrite
options.D: Ask Claude to confirm that its adaptation preserved every claim from the verified summary

rationale.correct: Adapting for an intended audience changes vocabulary, level of detail, and framing while leaving the claims intact — reformatting is never a correctness fix, and a claim that changed in adaptation needs re-verification. The strengthened statistic is now a different claim from the one that was verified.

distractors.A: Verification attaches to claims, not documents; assuming it survives a rewording that changed a claim is exactly the unchecked assumption.
distractors.B: Full re-evaluation of every variant spends review on claims that did not change; the discipline targets the ones that did.
distractors.D: The adapter confirming its own adaptation is self-review; the changed statistic needs checking against the source, not a reassurance.

questions.question: A trade marketing associate at a consumer goods company has two candidate promotional one-pagers, produced from different prompts, for a retailer meeting. The team gathers to choose between them. What is the most appropriate way to run the comparison?

options.A: Read both and select whichever reads more fluently end to end
options.B: State the criterion the one-pager must satisfy before reading, then judge both candidates against it
options.C: Circulate both versions and adopt the one most teammates prefer on a quick vote
options.D: Pick the version closer in style to the flashier deck a competing brand showed the retailer

rationale.correct: To compare outputs you need a stated criterion decided before reading them; without one, the most fluent candidate wins by default and the comparison is theatre. The criterion — what the retailer meeting must achieve — is fixed first, and both one-pagers are judged against it.

distractors.A: Fluency is the default winner precisely because no criterion was set; reading well and serving the meeting are different properties.
distractors.C: A preference vote samples opinions, not the requirement; the majority can favor the candidate that serves the meeting worse.
distractors.D: Imitating a competitor's style substitutes spectacle for the decision framework; nothing ties that style to this retailer's decision.

questions.question: A studio manager at a packaging design studio has Claude turn client briefs into production specifications — dimensions, materials, finishes — delivered as flowing prose. The production team re-keys the values into their system, and transcription errors keep surfacing at the printer. Which change is the most appropriate?

options.A: Keep the prose format and proofread each specification more carefully before handoff
options.B: Ask for longer prose descriptions in which every dimension is stated twice for safety
options.C: Have the key values printed in bold within the prose so they stand out when re-keyed
options.D: Deliver the specifications as structured data whose fields the production system takes directly

rationale.correct: To select appropriate output formats, choose by how the result will be used and how reliably it must hold: these values are consumed by a system, so structured data removes the re-keying step where the errors arise, and a field that fails is visible in a way prose never makes it.

distractors.A: Closer proofreading polices the symptom while the format still forces manual transcription of every value.
distractors.B: Stating dimensions twice doubles the prose to transcribe; volume is not reliability, and the re-keying step remains.
distractors.C: Bolding is presentation; the numbers are still carried in prose and still re-keyed by hand at the same risk.

questions.question: An operations lead at a specialty coffee importer built a Claude workflow that summarizes supplier contracts for the buying team. It was tested on five sample contracts the team wrote for the trial, every summary passed, and the lead plans to roll it out. Real supplier contracts arrive scanned, sometimes incomplete, and occasionally with clauses that contradict each other. What should happen before rollout?

options.A: Proceed: five passes out of five is a strong evaluation result for a workflow of this size
options.B: Extend the trial by writing five more sample contracts in the same style and testing those
options.C: Rebuild the evaluation sample from real supplier contracts, including incomplete and contradictory ones
options.D: Roll out now and monitor the buying team's complaints to find any summary problems

rationale.correct: An evaluation sample must represent production conditions — including missing, conflicting, and adversarial inputs. Team-written contracts are clean by construction, so the five passes evaluate a workflow the buying team will never actually run; real scanned, incomplete, contradictory contracts are the test that means something.

distractors.A: Five clean passes measure performance on inputs production will not send; the result is real but answers the wrong question.
distractors.B: More samples from the same clean distribution adds volume, not representativeness; the blind spots are inherited, not fixed.
distractors.D: Complaints are a lagging signal read off the buying team's failures; the evaluation belongs before rollout, not after.

questions.question: A member services lead at a credit union runs the same Claude request for rate-explanation letters twice and gets noticeably different letters; one draft also describes the same fee two ways in different paragraphs. One teammate wants it reported as a product defect; another says nothing can be done. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Treat variation as inherent: add a structural review step and set a measured consistency bound the letters must meet
options.B: File a defect report, since repeated runs of the same request should return identical letters
options.C: Withdraw Claude from member letters, as output that varies between runs cannot be used safely
options.D: Keep both grains of inconsistency in check by hand-aligning each letter to the latest approved template after generation

rationale.correct: Inconsistencies have two grains — two parts of one output disagreeing, and repeated runs disagreeing — and variation is inherent to the tool. Because output varies by design, the response is structural review built into the workflow plus a measured consistency bound, not a bug report and not resignation.

distractors.B: Run-to-run variation is designed behavior, not a defect; the report asserts a determinism the tool never promised.
distractors.C: Resignation discards the capability over a property that review and a consistency bound manage routinely.
distractors.D: Hand-aligning every letter treats each symptom downstream; the workflow itself still lacks the review step and the bound.

questions.question: A production coordinator at a film production coordination office reviews a week's batch of Claude-drafted daily call sheets: 96% of entries are accurate, above the team's 95% target, but one sheet listed the wrong stunt safety contact. A colleague proposes accepting the batch on its average. What is the most appropriate call?

options.A: Accept the batch: 96% exceeds the 95% target the team set for call-sheet accuracy
options.B: Treat the safety-contact error as a stop condition: hold the batch, find the cause, and re-review
options.C: Ship the sheets with a standing note asking crew members to confirm safety contacts themselves
options.D: Correct the one wrong sheet, ship the rest unchanged, and leave the process as it is

rationale.correct: A severity-class failure is not tradable against an aggregate quality score: one prohibited error in a batch is a stop condition even when the average looks excellent. A wrong stunt safety contact is in the prohibited class, so the batch holds until the cause is found and the sheets are re-reviewed.

distractors.A: The 95% target governs ordinary errors; averaging a prohibited safety error against routine accuracy is the exact trade the rule forbids.
distractors.C: Asking crew to verify contacts pushes the failure onto the people the sheet exists to protect.
distractors.D: Fixing the single instance leaves the mechanism that produced it unexamined; the next wrong contact ships on schedule.

questions.question: A bid coordinator at an architecture firm runs every Claude task in a plain chat out of habit — including a bid-review task that recurs every few weeks and requires re-uploading the same firm boilerplate, past project summaries, and style guide at the start of each session. The re-uploading is eating time and sessions start inconsistently. What is the most appropriate move?

options.A: Stay in chat and keep a ready-made snippet of the boilerplate to paste in faster each session
options.B: Stay in chat and paste in even more firm context each session so no detail is ever missing
options.C: Switch to whichever surface a partner firm mentioned works well for their bid reviews
options.D: Choose the entry point from the task's shape first, then build the prompt for that surface

rationale.correct: The entry point is selected before the prompt is written, because the surface determines what context is available and what the output can be. Recurring work with stable context is a task shape with a surface built for it; choosing by habit is exactly the failure this decision exists to prevent.

distractors.A: A paste snippet speeds up the workaround without questioning it; every session still rebuilds context a better surface would hold.
distractors.B: More pasted context enlarges each session's setup; volume does not fix a task sitting on the wrong surface.
distractors.C: Another firm's mention is an anecdote about their tasks; the surface is chosen from this task's shape, not from hearsay.

questions.question: A membership officer at an art museum needs a comparison of how a dozen peer institutions currently price and structure their membership tiers, drawing on each institution's latest published offering. The officer is deciding where to run the task. Which choice best fits the task?

options.A: Run it in research mode, matching a task that needs current information from many sources
options.B: Run it anywhere, as every surface reaches the same information and the choice is cosmetic
options.C: Set up a dedicated Project with uploaded knowledge and standing instructions before starting
options.D: Run it in a plain chat and draw the comparison from the model's built-in knowledge

rationale.correct: The four surfaces answer four different problems — chat for one-off work, Projects for recurring work with stable context, artifacts for deliverable outputs, and research mode for tasks needing current multi-source information. A dozen institutions' latest published offerings is squarely the research mode problem.

distractors.B: The surfaces differ in exactly what this task needs — what information they can reach; the claim that they are interchangeable invents an equivalence.
distractors.C: A Project suits recurring work with stable context; standing up one for a one-off comparison is setup with no recurring payoff.
distractors.D: A plain chat leans on built-in knowledge for facts that are current and scattered across many sources — the one problem shape it does not answer.

questions.question: An events coordinator at a botanical garden drafts sponsor thank-you letters with Claude about twice a quarter, and the events manager reviews each letter before it goes out. A teammate proposes commissioning an automated agent pipeline connected to the sponsor database so the letters generate and send themselves. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Adopt the proposal and build the automated pipeline with the database connection
options.B: Hand the entire letters task to the IT team so they can decide how to build and own it
options.C: Keep the letters in the interactive surface with the manager's review, and skip the automation
options.D: Adopt the automation for the visibility it gives the office when the sponsor board hears of it

rationale.correct: For occasional, human-reviewed work with no integration requirement, the interactive surface is the right answer. Automation here is a cost with no payer — twice a quarter, already reviewed — and building an agent pipeline sits beyond Associate scope besides; the moment to escalate is when a real integration need appears.

distractors.A: An agent pipeline adds machinery a twice-a-quarter reviewed task cannot repay, and removes the review that makes the letters safe.
distractors.B: Handing the whole task away defers a decision the coordinator can already make; nothing here needs IT to own letter writing.
distractors.D: Board visibility is spectacle, not a decision criterion; the task's shape, volume, and review need have not changed.

questions.question: A finance associate at a building materials distributor is setting up Claude for monthly rebate statements. Two needs are on the table: the statements must follow the team's exact multi-step checking procedure the same way every month, and the rebate totals must be verifiably correct rather than plausible. Which TWO capability layers address these two needs? (Select TWO.)

options.A: A Skill that defines the team's checking procedure so it runs the same way each month
options.B: Memory, so the way earlier statements were handled carries over month to month
options.C: Running each statement twice in separate chats and keeping the totals that match
options.D: Code Execution, so the rebate totals are computed rather than generated
options.E: An added instruction telling the model to be especially meticulous with arithmetic

rationale.correct: The four capability layers own four distinct jobs — Projects carry context, Skills define repeatable procedures, Code Execution verifies computation, Memory persists continuity. The two stated needs are a repeatable procedure and verified computation, which map to a Skill and to Code Execution; combining layers is fine, substituting one for another is not.

distractors.B: Memory persists continuity across sessions; it does not define or enforce a procedure, so the checking steps would still drift.
distractors.C: Two generated runs agreeing measures consistency, not correctness — both can carry the same wrong total.
distractors.E: An exhortation to be meticulous changes register, not mechanism; generated arithmetic stays generated.

questions.question: A leasing operations manager at a commercial real estate firm is assigning model tiers to three workloads: extracting standard terms from hundreds of routine lease documents, everyday drafting and analysis for the leasing team, and a complex portfolio consolidation strategy where quality matters far more than speed. Which assignment best fits the three workloads?

options.A: The most capable tier for all three workloads, so no task is ever under-served
options.B: Haiku for the high-volume extraction, Sonnet for the everyday work, Opus for the consolidation strategy
options.C: The fastest, lowest-cost tier for all three workloads to keep the program's spend minimal
options.D: Whichever tier answers quickest in a short trial on each workload, measured with a stopwatch

rationale.correct: The three tiers trade speed and cost against capability, each with a characteristic task shape: Haiku for structured high-volume work like the extraction, Sonnet for most professional work, and Opus for complex high-stakes work where quality outranks speed, like the consolidation strategy.

distractors.A: Maximum capability on structured bulk work spends cost and latency for nothing; capability is not a free upgrade.
distractors.C: Forcing the strategy work onto the lightest tier hits the cost goal by giving up the quality that workload exists to buy.
distractors.D: Response speed is one axis of a trade-off, not the decision; a stopwatch trial ignores what each workload demands.

questions.question: A registrar's office at a community college sends thousands of transcript-request acknowledgment emails each term — short, structured, high-volume work where speed and cost matter more than deep reasoning. In testing, both the lightest tier and the mid tier cleared the office's quality bar for these emails. Which selection is the most appropriate?

options.A: The most capable tier, so the office holds a quality margin beyond the bar it set
options.B: The tier whose test emails read the most polished when the team compared them side by side
options.C: The mid tier, as the recommended default for professional work of any kind
options.D: The fastest, lowest-cost tier that cleared the quality bar in the office's testing

rationale.correct: Once several tiers clear the quality bar the task actually requires, selection is a constrained optimization on cost and speed: the cheapest, fastest option that still meets the task requirements wins. Both tiers passed, so the lighter one is the correct choice for thousands of emails a term.

distractors.A: A margin beyond a bar the task already meets buys nothing; it converts cleared requirements into standing cost and latency.
distractors.B: Side-by-side polish is register; both tiers already cleared the bar that actually governs these emails.
distractors.C: A default is a starting point, not a verdict; applied after a lighter tier cleared the bar, it is dogma overriding the measured result.

questions.question: The operations team at a conference and exhibitions organizer routes every Claude task — including bulk attendee-list cleanups and simple confirmation drafts — to the most capable model tier, describing the habit as a safety margin. Turnaround on bulk jobs is slow and the program's costs are climbing. What is the most appropriate assessment?

options.A: Route straightforward bulk work to a lighter tier and reserve the top tier for tasks that need it
options.B: Keep the routing: the top tier also completes bulk work faster, so there is no trade-off to manage
options.C: Keep the routing and pack more attendee rows into each request so fewer requests are needed
options.D: Keep the routing, as maximum capability for everything is the prudent default for a serious program

rationale.correct: Defaulting to the most capable tier for everything is a cost and latency failure, not a safety margin. The speed-capability trade-off is real: capability is not a free upgrade, and over-provisioning straightforward work spends both cost and speed for nothing — exactly what the slow queue and climbing spend are showing.

distractors.B: The claim inverts the trade-off; the heaviest tier is not also the fastest, and the slow bulk queue is the evidence in hand.
distractors.C: Packing requests fuller optimizes around the mis-assignment; the work is still over-provisioned on every row.
distractors.D: Prudence that ignores measured cost and latency is a slogan; the default is producing the failure it claims to prevent.

questions.question: A sales planner at a craft brewery cooperative has kept one continuous Claude conversation running all week for seasonal planning — uploads, drafts, and revisions all in the same thread. By Friday the responses are noticeably weaker and earlier instructions are being dropped, and a teammate concludes the model itself has degraded. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: The model was silently swapped for a weaker version partway through the week
options.B: The requests need to be phrased more forcefully for the model to keep taking them seriously
options.C: The week-long conversation has been filling its finite context, degrading output gradually as it fills
options.D: The tool is unsuited to planning work, and the seasonal plan should be finished by hand

rationale.correct: Context is a budget: a long conversation degrades output quality as the budget fills, and the degradation is gradual enough to look like a model failure. That resemblance is why this is a diagnosis to reach — the week of accumulated uploads and drafts, not the model, explains Friday's weaker responses.

distractors.A: A silent midweek swap is an invented mechanism; the gradual decline tracks the conversation's growth, not a version change.
distractors.B: Forceful phrasing is a register knob; it does not recover a budget the conversation has already spent.
distractors.D: The tool handled Monday's planning well; abandoning it misreads a managed, finite budget as a fixed limitation.

questions.question: A pricing analyst at an e-bike rental operator is deep in a long Claude conversation exploring seasonal pricing. The conclusions reached so far will drive the next phase of work; the exploratory back-and-forth behind them will not be needed again. Quality has not dropped yet, but the conversation is growing fast. What is the most appropriate move?

options.A: Keep working in the thread until quality visibly drops, and decide what to do at that point
options.B: Summarize the conclusions now and carry them into a fresh session before quality slips
options.C: Start a clean session without carrying anything over, re-deriving conclusions if they come up
options.D: Stay in the same thread and rely on the long context to keep holding everything relevant

rationale.correct: The three context remedies are chosen by what must survive the transition: restart when nothing must, summarize when the conclusions must, persist when continuity must outlive the session. Here the conclusions must survive and the exploration need not — and the choice is made before quality visibly drops, not after.

distractors.A: Waiting for visible degradation makes the decision after damage begins; the discipline is to decide early, while the choice is still cheap.
distractors.C: A bare restart discards the conclusions the next phase depends on; re-deriving them repays work already done.
distractors.D: Leaning on a growing thread spends a finite budget toward exactly the degradation the analyst can see coming.

questions.question: A committee secretary at an engineering standards secretariat is confused: details discussed in yesterday's Claude session are missing from today's, yet some working preferences do seem to carry over between sessions. The secretary wants a reliable mental model before configuring anything further. Which understanding is the most appropriate?

options.A: Everything from every past session is retained and automatically recalled whenever it is relevant
options.B: Cross-session continuity should not be relied on at all, and each session must rebuild from documents
options.C: Writing the committee's standing rules into each day's first message is how continuity is maintained
options.D: The context window carries the current conversation; Memory persists continuity across sessions

rationale.correct: Memory is a distinct mechanism from the conversation's context window: the context window carries the current session, while Memory persists continuity across sessions. Confusing the two misroutes both configuration and diagnosis — which is exactly the confusion the missing-details puzzle is exposing.

distractors.A: Total recall of every past session is an invented mechanism; what persists is what the continuity layer holds, not everything said.
distractors.B: Refusing continuity altogether discards a mechanism that exists for the job; the fix is understanding it, not abandoning it.
distractors.C: Restating standing rules per session parks a durable requirement in the most transient mechanism available — the wrong layer for it.

questions.question: An operations associate at a facilities management contractor has a folder of stakeholder emails, complaint threads, and meeting notes about a new maintenance-request process, and wants Claude's help turning the mess into something the implementation team can act on. Which request makes the best use of the tool here?

options.A: Ask for a short readable summary of what the stakeholders seem to want overall
options.B: Ask for structured requirements, each traceable to its source input and testable by the team
options.C: Ask Claude to design the entire new maintenance-request process end to end from the folder
options.D: Ask for a first-pass requirements narrative and circulate it as final if it reads complete

rationale.correct: Requirements analysis is the canonical delegation of analysis work: messy stakeholder input becomes structured, traceable, testable requirements that others can act on. The output is a working artefact — each requirement traceable to a source and testable — not a summary of sentiment.

distractors.A: A summary flattens the mess into prose; it drops the structure and traceability the implementation team needs to act.
distractors.C: Designing the whole process leaps past the analysis step and hands over decisions the stakeholders have not yet made.
distractors.D: Reading complete is register; a requirements set is judged by whether each item is traceable and testable, not by its flow.

questions.question: A planning officer at a ferry and harbor operations authority is deciding which steps of the seasonal timetable process to hand to Claude. A colleague asks what property should qualify a step for delegation in the first place. Which criterion is the most appropriate?

options.A: Steps where the tool's output consistently reads reliable and assured
options.B: Steps that other harbor operators mention they already delegate successfully
options.C: Steps whose output the team can check before anything downstream consumes it
options.D: Steps that are repetitive, as repetitive work is always appropriate to delegate

rationale.correct: A step is safe to delegate when its output can be checked: checkability, not confidence in the tool, is the qualifying property. A checkable output lets the team verify each result before it is used, which is what keeps the delegated step trustworthy.

distractors.A: An assured register is not a property of the step; it is how wrong output looks as well as right output.
distractors.B: Other operators' habits are anecdotes about their workflows and their risk tolerances, not a criterion for this one.
distractors.D: Repetitive is a slogan, not a safety property; a repetitive step whose output cannot be checked is still unsafe to hand over.

questions.question: A scheduling manager at a food safety auditing firm is building the annual audit-capacity plan with Claude: a narrative for the leadership team, resting on auditor-day totals and utilization percentages derived from the firm's booking export. The manager is deciding how the plan should be produced. Which design is the most appropriate?

options.A: Generate the whole plan, then schedule a fact-check of the figures just before publication
options.B: Base the figures on last year's utilization as the team remembers it, and generate the narrative
options.C: Give the model more of the firm's spreadsheets so its generated estimates land closer
options.D: Pair the synthesis with code execution so the figures are computed from the export as the plan is built

rationale.correct: Plans are built on verified numbers: the synthesis may be generated, but the figures underneath are computed — and pairing generation with code execution is a design choice made when the plan is built, not a check bolted on afterwards.

distractors.A: An end-stage fact-check inspects generated figures after the plan is shaped around them; the design decision was to compute them.
distractors.B: Remembered utilization is an assumption standing in for the booking export the firm actually holds.
distractors.C: More spreadsheets feed better guesses; the figures are still generated, and closeness is not verification.

questions.question: A coordinator at a hospice volunteer program wants to point Claude at the program's biggest time sink, which the coordinator is sure is the scheduling email back-and-forth. Nothing about the workflow has been measured. What should happen before any step is delegated?

options.A: Instrument the workflow to find where the time actually goes, then aim Claude at the friction that shows up
options.B: Proceed on the coordinator's recollection, which comes from living inside the workflow daily
options.C: Automate the whole volunteer workflow at once so every possible time sink is covered
options.D: Delegate the scheduling emails now and watch the quarterly volunteer survey for improvement

rationale.correct: You cannot optimize what is not instrumented at the level where the cause lives. Process optimization starts from an instrumented workflow, so the friction being removed is the real one and not the remembered one — the certainty about scheduling emails is exactly the assumption the measurement exists to test.

distractors.B: Living inside a workflow produces vivid impressions, not measurements; the loudest annoyance is often not the largest cost.
distractors.C: Automating everything to avoid choosing spends effort across steps that were never the friction, and removes checkpoints besides.
distractors.D: A quarterly survey is a lagging, indirect readout; it cannot attribute any change to the step that was delegated.

questions.question: A course designer at an industrial safety training company develops new curricula with Claude in stages — outline, module drafts, assessments — reviewing each stage before the next begins. A manager proposes handing the whole design over in one pass to save review time, since the drafts have been strong. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Adopt the single-pass handover and recover the review hours the stages were consuming
options.B: Adopt the single-pass handover but review the finished curriculum thoroughly at the end
options.C: Keep the delegation stepwise, with a checkpoint where human judgment re-enters at each stage
options.D: Keep the stages but skip the checkpoints on drafts that come back reading polished

rationale.correct: Design work is delegated step by step with checkpoints rather than handed over whole — each checkpoint is where human judgment re-enters, and removing them is what turns support into abdication. For safety curricula, the checkpoints are the mechanism that keeps errors from compounding across stages.

distractors.A: Recovered hours are bought by removing every point where judgment could intervene; strong past drafts do not retire that need.
distractors.B: One review at the end inspects a finished structure whose early-stage errors every later stage has already built on.
distractors.D: Polish is register, not correctness; skipping checkpoints for confident-looking drafts filters review by exactly the wrong signal.

questions.question: An internal communications manager reviews a Claude-assisted intranet redesign proposal built to the department's brief. The information architecture is strong, but the tone-of-voice section misses the company's plain-language standard. A teammate suggests starting the whole proposal again. What is the most appropriate next round?

options.A: Revise the architecture, tone, and scope together so the next version improves everywhere at once
options.B: Keep the architecture and rework only the tone-of-voice section the review identified
options.C: Take the design back from the tool and rewrite the proposal by hand from the brief
options.D: Shelve the proposal and revisit the redesign in next quarter's planning cycle

rationale.correct: Iteration on a delegated design follows the same diagnostic loop as prompt iteration: the result names the component that failed — here the tone-of-voice section — and that component, not the whole design, is what changes in the next round. The strong architecture is kept, and the fix is attributable.

distractors.A: Changing everything at once discards working material and makes the next version's gains and losses unattributable.
distractors.C: Abandoning the delegation over one failed section throws away a strong architecture and the diagnostic the review produced.
distractors.D: Deferral leaves a nearly-right proposal idle; the review already named the one section standing between it and done.

questions.question: An operations manager at a landscaping services franchise is bringing Claude into the quoting workflow: site notes are summarized, materials are itemized, prices are calculated against the rate card, and a franchise owner approves each quote before it is sent. A consultant proposes automating the workflow end to end, approval included. What is the most appropriate design?

options.A: Choose the steps Claude performs and keep the owner's approval checkpoint in place
options.B: Automate every step including the approval so quotes leave the system untouched
options.C: Automate whichever steps will make the demonstration most impressive at the franchise convention
options.D: Keep Claude out of the quoting workflow entirely so the question of automation never arises

rationale.correct: The value in a workflow comes from choosing which steps Claude performs — the discipline is to delegate deliberately, not automate indiscriminately. A workflow handed over whole loses the checkpoints that made it trustworthy, and the owner's approval is exactly such a checkpoint.

distractors.B: End-to-end automation grants autonomy the quoting process does not need and removes the approval that catches a bad quote before a customer sees it.
distractors.C: Convention spectacle is not a selection criterion; steps are chosen by value and checkability, not by demo impact.
distractors.D: Refusing every step forfeits the real gains in summarizing and itemizing; the checkpoint question had a better answer than abstinence.

questions.question: An admissions manager at a language school is mapping the enrollment workflow — inquiry replies, placement-test scoring, offer letters, visa-document checks — to decide Claude's role in each step. Which classification approach is the most appropriate?

options.A: Sort the steps into two bins, automate or keep, so the mapping stays simple to run
options.B: Classify by which steps the admissions staff most dislike doing by hand
options.C: Adopt the step classification a conference speaker presented for language schools
options.D: Rate each step on reversibility, stakes, and accountability, and classify it as AI-appropriate, human-retained, or collaborative

rationale.correct: Each workflow step is classified against reversibility, stakes, and accountability into a three-way verdict — AI-appropriate, human-retained, or collaborative — and the middle verdict is the common one. A visa-document check and an inquiry reply land differently on all three criteria, which is the point of rating each step.

distractors.A: A two-bin sort deletes the collaborative middle where most real steps belong, forcing them into over- or under-delegation.
distractors.B: Staff preference measures comfort, not risk; the steps people most want to hand off can be the ones the criteria retain.
distractors.C: A conference template is someone else's mapping; the criteria have to be applied to this school's steps and stakes.

questions.question: A procurement officer at a mining site is adding Claude to the purchase-order workflow: requests are drafted and validated, and a released purchase order is an irreversible payment commitment. The team is designing the human approval gate. Which TWO properties must the gate have? (Select TWO.)

options.A: It sits immediately after each purchase order releases, so errors are caught quickly
options.B: It sits after validation and before the irreversible release
options.C: It clears by default after four hours so the workflow never stalls on an absent approver
options.D: It records every release in a log the office reviews at the end of each month
options.E: It has a named gatekeeper who is accountable for staffing the decision

rationale.correct: The approval gate sits after validation and before the irreversible action, and it must have a real gatekeeper. A gate placed after the release reviews a payment already committed, and a gate nobody staffs is not a control — position and a named, accountable gatekeeper are the two properties that make it one.

distractors.A: After release, the commitment is already made; a fast catch of an irreversible action is a report, not a gate.
distractors.C: A default-clear timeout is the gate approving by absence; the workflow never stalls because the control never operates.
distractors.D: A monthly log review is a lagging record of what already left; it informs trends and stops nothing.

questions.question: A team lead at a paralegal support bureau is designing Claude's role in court-filing preparation, a process with fixed steps in a fixed order and a fixed validation checklist at each step. A colleague proposes granting the tool open-ended autonomy to find the best approach for each filing, pointing to an impressive pilot demonstration. Which design is the most appropriate?

options.A: Grant broad autonomy and add more tools so the approach can adapt filing by filing
options.B: Grant autonomy as the modern default, since agent-style designs are where the field is heading
options.C: Mirror the fixed steps and validation in an explicit, structured workflow, granting autonomy nowhere it is not needed
options.D: Adopt the autonomous design on the strength of the pilot demonstration the colleague showed

rationale.correct: A process with fixed steps and fixed validation argues for an explicit, structured workflow; autonomy is granted only where the process actually needs it, never as a default posture. Court filings are the strong case: the order and the checklist are the requirement, and the design should enforce them.

distractors.A: Adaptability is the property this process is required not to have; more tools and latitude loosen exactly what the checklist fixes.
distractors.B: Where the field is heading is a slogan; this process's binding constraint is fixed order and fixed validation, which points the other way.
distractors.D: A demonstration is a curated best run; it measures nothing about how open-ended autonomy behaves across a docket of real filings.

questions.question: A communications officer at a port authority needs Claude to draft notices to mariners from incident reports. The stated requirement: drafts that follow the notice template, reviewed by the duty officer before publication. An enthusiastic teammate sketches a pipeline that generates several candidate drafts in parallel, scores them against a rubric, and auto-selects a winner. Which design should the officer choose?

options.A: A single drafting step against the template, followed by the duty officer's review
options.B: The parallel-drafts pipeline with rubric scoring and automatic selection
options.C: The pipeline, as its sophistication will demonstrate the program's rigor to leadership
options.D: A middle path that generates five drafts per notice for the duty officer to choose among

rationale.correct: Complexity in a solution design is justified by requirements, never by ambition or the appearance of rigor. The stated requirement is template-true drafts plus duty-officer review; the simplest design that meets the stated requirement is the professional answer, and the single step with review is that design.

distractors.B: Parallel generation, scoring, and auto-selection answer requirements nobody stated; the machinery adds failure modes, not fitness.
distractors.C: Impressing leadership is ambition wearing an engineering costume; rigor is meeting the requirement, not displaying apparatus.
distractors.D: Five drafts per notice quintuples review load for a template task; volume is not a requirement anyone set.

questions.question: A program manager at a professional certification body is briefing the executive team on a Claude rollout for candidate communications, and wants the briefing to earn durable trust rather than a quick yes. Which TWO elements belong in the briefing? (Select TWO.)

options.A: The capability claims stated together with their limits
options.B: The human review gates that make the claimed capabilities safe to rely on
options.C: A version of the briefing that leaves the limits out so adoption is not discouraged
options.D: Sample outputs selected for how impressive they read in front of executives
options.E: A year-end commitment to fully automated candidate communications with no review step

rationale.correct: Capability claims are stated together with their limits and the human review gates that make them safe. Overstating value is the stakeholder-trust failure, and accurate limits are what earn the trust back — a briefing built on claims-with-limits plus the gates is the one that survives contact with the first imperfect output.

distractors.C: Omitting the limits to smooth adoption is silent overstatement; the trust it buys is spent the first time an output falls short.
distractors.D: Hand-picked impressive samples are demo theatre; they measure the curator's taste, not the system the executives are approving.
distractors.E: A no-review automation pledge grants the program autonomy nobody requires and stakes its credibility on removing the gates that protect it.

questions.question: A delivery lead at a recruitment process outsourcing firm has configured Claude Projects and prompts that produce excellent candidate summaries. The operations director now asks the lead to also build an API integration that pushes each summary automatically into the client's applicant tracking system. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.A: Build the integration personally, using shared administrator credentials the client once provided
options.B: Deliver the Projects and prompt work, and escalate the API integration to a Claude Developer
options.C: Escalate the entire request, including the Projects and prompt work already in hand
options.D: Deliver the Projects and prompt work, and let the integration half of the request quietly lapse

rationale.correct: Recognizing the edge of Associate scope is itself a competency: API integration belongs to a Claude Developer, and the professional move is to do the in-scope part and escalate the rest. Both polarities are errors — attempting the build personally and handing away work that is squarely in scope.

distractors.A: A self-built integration on borrowed administrator credentials crosses the scope boundary and widens the client's exposure while it does.
distractors.C: Escalating work the lead is qualified to finish is over-escalation; the summaries and configuration are exactly Associate-scope deliverables.
distractors.D: Letting the request lapse without saying so absorbs the scope problem silently; the director decides next steps only if told the boundary exists.
